info.bio: Los integrantes del grupo "The Animals" eran originarios de la localidad portuaria de Newcastle-upon-Tyne en el noreste de Inglaterra. La creación del grupo data del 1962 cuando Eric Burdon se unió a la "Alan Price Rhythm and Blues Combo", que cambió desde entonces su nombre por el de "The Animals". Su música se basaba esencialmente en el blues y rhythm and blues y se dedicaban a hacer versiones de canciones de John Lee Hooker, Sam Cooke, Ray Charles, Nina Simone y Jimmy Reed.

scenes.name: Beat, R&B y mod pop británico
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Tras el éxito de los Beatles, las cuatro grandes discográficas (EMI, Decca, Pye y Philips) saquearon metódicamente las provincias: firmaban barato y esperaban a ver qué pegaba. Pye, del veterano Louis Benjamin, tenía a los Kinks y a los Searchers y fama de contratos miserables. Los Ugly’s de Birmingham, nacidos del skiffle y curtidos en los clubes alemanes, se distinguían por su conciencia social; la cara B de su tercer single, «A Quiet Explosion» (21 de enero de 1966), con órgano Vox Continental, un riff con eco a lo Delia Derbyshire y un bajo descendente que es la bomba cayendo, desapareció en la sobreproducción del momento, pero es un disco extraño y auténtico que se acerca a la psicodelia. A principios de 1966 las bases del beat y del R&B se llevaron al límite, como bajo una enorme presión: «Keep on Running» de Spencer Davis casa soul y mod pop, los Wheels de Belfast aceleran sin freno en «Bad Little Woman» y los Poets de Glasgow, de Andrew Loog Oldham, desquician el «Baby Don’t You Do It» de Marvin Gaye.

podcast.title: Alan Price's Abrupt Departure
podcast.body: On April 28, 1965, Alan Price abruptly left The Animals on the day of a European tour. Charles Chandler, his flatmate, believed Price's first royalty check for "House of the Rising Sun" arrived that morning, prompting Price to unilaterally decide not to share the money as previously agreed. Chandler did not see Price for 18 months afterward. "Chandler believed until his death that while he was in the shower, Price's first royalty check for arranging House of the Rising Sunhood arrived, and Price had decided then and there that he wasn't going to share the money as agreed."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Alan Price's Integration and Musical Tensions
podcast.body: Alan Price joined the group on piano and immediately "jelled," despite Eric Burden and John Steele finding his musical tastes "pedestrian" and regarding him as a "lounge player" compared to their own "hipper" R&B and blues preferences. This tension was an ongoing factor within the band. "The other members would always like to say that they didn't like Price either as a person or for his taste in music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Art School Origins in Newcastle
podcast.body: Like many British bands of the era, The Animals' story began at an art school in Newcastle, where Eric Burden and John Steele first met. Newcastle's isolation as a major city fostered a unique local music scene, limiting musician options and encouraging bands to play within their immediate region. "The story of the animals, like so many of the British bands of this time period, starts at art school, where two teenagers named Eric Burden and John Steele met each other."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 115: "House of the Rising Sun" by the Animals

podcast.title: Backing Sonny Boy Williamson II
podcast.body: The group, then known as The Alan Price Rhythm and Blues Combo, performed live backing the prominent American blues musician Sonny Boy Williamson II at Newcastle's Club a Go-Go. This performance was recorded and showcased their distinctive electric organ sound, which impressed Graham Bond. "That sound can be heard and alive recording of them a couple of months later, backing the great American blues musician Sonny Boy Williamson II, at the club of Go Go."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 115: "House of the Rising Sun" by the Animals

podcast.title: Break with Mickey Most
podcast.body: The Animals eventually severed ties with producer Mickey Most, citing their dissatisfaction with his persistent efforts to push them towards a more pop-oriented sound. They subsequently signed with Decca Records and enlisted Tom Wilson as their new producer. "The group were getting sick of most attempts to make them more poppy."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 115: "House of the Rising Sun" by the Animals

podcast.title: Controversial Name Change
podcast.body: When the group played London gigs in December 1963, they were billed as The Animals. Members could never agree on how the name originated, and not all of them liked it. "None of the members of the group could ever agree on how they got their new name, and not all of them liked it."

podcast.title: Deep Voice with Acute Guitars (1960s)
podcast.body: Eric Burdon, despite possessing an incredibly potent and deep vocal register in the 1960s, still performed with guitars that sounded acute. This demonstrates how pervasive this guitar characteristic was, even when paired with diverse vocal styles, prior to Led Zeppelin's revolutionary sound. "Eric Borden, andé animales en los 60 a pesar de la increíble resistor potente que tenía Eric Borden sus guitarras sonaban así."

podcast.title: Dispute Over "House of the Rising Sun" Royalties
podcast.body: The group's manager, Mike Jeffery, allegedly told The Animals that only one name could be credited as arranger for their public domain song "House of the Rising Sun," but that royalties would be shared. Alan Price, however, was the sole credited arranger and the only one to receive songwriting royalties, which became a significant source of contention. "Whatever the truth, Price was the only one who ever got any songwriting royalties from their version of the song, which went to number 1 in the UK and the US."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Dylan's "Stolen Song" Accusation
podcast.body: The Animals' hit version of "House of the Rising Sun" ironically led to Bob Dylan dropping the song from his own live set, as audiences frequently asked him if he had stolen it from The Animals, providing Dave Van Ronk (from whom Dylan learned the arrangement) "the last laugh." "Incidentally Dave Van Runk had the last laugh at Dylan, who had to drop the song from his own set because people kept asking him if he'd stolen it from the animals."

podcast.title: Evolution from Jazz to R&B
podcast.body: Eric Burden and John Steele initially formed a trad jazz band called The Pagan Jazzmen. With the rise of rock and roll and skiffle, they transformed into The Pagans R&B Band, shifting to a guitar-based lineup with Steele on drums and Burden as lead singer. "Steel and burden, when they met at art school, were both jazz fanatics, and they quickly formed a trad jazz band."

podcast.title: Following Hawkins' Musical Path
podcast.body: The Animals are identified as one of the 1960s white rock acts that followed in Dale Hawkins' musical footsteps. Their sound incorporated elements such as electric bass, Chess-style guitar riffs, and country-inflected vocals, which were pioneered and featured in Hawkins' "Suzy Q." "Acts like the Rolling Stones or the Animals or Cand Heat were all following in Hawkins' footsteps"

podcast.title: Management Fraud and Disappearance of Funds
podcast.body: The original group ultimately dissolved, discovering they had been extensively defrauded by their management. A tax-saving scheme involving banking their money in the Bahamas resulted in the mysterious disappearance of the bank and, consequently, their funds. "There had been a scheme to bank their money in the Bahamas for tax reasons, in a bank which mysteriously disappeared off the face of the earth."

podcast.title: Mickey Most's First Signing
podcast.body: The Animals were the first band signed by independent producer Mickey Most upon his return to the UK in 1963, following a successful period producing cover versions in South Africa. Most licensed their records to EMI, and the band moved to London in January 1964. "the animals were his first signing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Reunions and Later Formations
podcast.body: The original lineup of The Animals reunited sporadically between 1968 and the early 1980s, with their final performance together in 1983. Eric Burden went on to form "The New Animals" and "Eric Burdon and the Animals." John Steele, Dave Rowberry, and Hilton Valentine reformed a version in the 1990s, with Steele continuing to tour as "The Animals and Friends." "There were a handful of reunions of the original lineup of the group, between 1968 and the early 80s, but they last played together in 1983."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Unusual Single Length
podcast.body: "House of the Rising Sun" was 4 minutes and 20 seconds long, exceeding the customary 3-minute limit for radio singles. Producer Mickey Most was eventually persuaded by Charles Chandler to release the track unedited, a bold decision for the time. "The record was 4 minutes and 20 seconds long, and you just didn't ever release a record that long."

xref.title: "The Eggman" Nickname Origin
xref.body: Eric Burdon, the leader of The Animals, acquired the nickname "the Eggman" after he disclosed details of an unusual oral sex act involving raw eggs, which he learned from his Jamaican girlfriend, Sylvia. This anecdote later found its way into The Beatles' song "I Am the Walrus," with John Lennon adopting the moniker. "And when he told everybody about it, he was immediately nicknamed the Eggman."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 60 Mind-Blowing Things About Music: 2021 Edition

xref.title: Dave Gahan's Paranoia and Delusions
xref.body: Amidst his severe drug addiction, Dave Gahan developed extreme paranoia, leading him to carry a gun even for routine tasks like walking from his house to the mailbox. His mental state deteriorated into delusional behavior, including watching the Weather Channel for 24 consecutive hours, painting his walls and floor black, and engaging in conversations with his collection of stuffed animals, a behavior that became concerning when he claimed the animals began to speak back to him. "He grew paranoid and carried a gun, even just to get from the house to the mailbox."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Who Lost It: Part 2

xref.title: Discovery and Formation in England
xref.body: Jimi Hendrix was discovered at 22 years old in Greenwich Village, New York. He was subsequently invited by the manager of The Animals to audition for a new group being formed in England, which led to the formation of The Jimi Hendrix Experience. "Jimmy's 22 years old and was discovered in Greenwich Village, New York and invited by the manager of the animals to audition for a new group being formed in England."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 2

xref.title: Extensive Pre-Police Career
xref.body: Prior to joining The Police, Andy Summers had an extensive career playing in bands since the mid-1960s, working as a studio musician, and backing other artists on tour, including a stint with The Animals in 1968. "He had been playing in band since the mid-1960s. He was also a studio guy and a guitarist who backed up other artists with their touring bands. That included a stint in the animals back in 1968."
